project.title: Unobravo Redesign
project.description: A research-led redesign of Unobravo's website and app that makes starting online therapy easier to understand, compare and trust.
project.introText: Unobravo connects people with therapists over video call. Its website tried to be a marketing page, a guide and an onboarding flow at once, and the app offered no explanation of the service at all. I redesigned both, from interviews to a tested Figma prototype. A concept redesign made for an HCI course; not affiliated with Unobravo.
project.middleText: The research combined interviews across three age groups, a competitor study of Serenis, expert reviews and think-aloud testing. It surfaced nine usability issues: an overwhelming "how it works" page, calls to action that pushed people into the questionnaire before they understood the service, opaque therapist matching, scheduling that ignored stated preferences, a full test to repeat just to change therapist, no way to compare profiles, hidden pricing and privacy information, and an app whose navigation was buried in a sidebar.
project.conclusionText: Over three iterations the design added a calmer home page, a real dashboard with the next appointment and pricing, three therapist proposals with a "why you match" explanation, filters to compare profiles, and a way to change therapist by only updating preferences. In the summative test of the final version, all four participants completed every task with no errors, and the average SUS score rose from 75 on the original product to 91.25.

context.text: Unobravo is a leading European online psychology service, founded in Italy in 2019, that matches people with licensed therapists over video call. Many potential users hesitate: they worry about privacy, doubt that online therapy can feel human, and don't understand how the matching works. The goal was to reduce that reluctance and make the service easy to understand and trust, across ages and levels of digital literacy.

goals.title: Transparency
goals.text: Explain data practices, pricing and the matching process clearly, so privacy concerns can be resolved rather than hidden in a footer.

goals.title: Personalization
goals.text: Adapt the journey to different needs and levels of readiness, from someone just exploring to someone ready to book.

methods.title: Segmentation
methods.text: Three age groups (25-34, 35-44, 45-55) crossed with the Stages of Change model. The focus segment: young adults in the Preparation stage.

methods.title: Interviews and market research
methods.text: Four young adults, two mid-career and two mature adults, plus published data on Gen Z mental health, stigma and access to support.

methods.title: Expert review
methods.text: Direct and reverse checkpoint reviews of Unobravo and its competitor Serenis, on website and app.

methods.title: Preliminary testing
methods.text: Four tasks on each product: understand the service, take the matching test, change therapist, compare profiles. SUS on the original: 75.

methods.title: Service blueprint and information architecture
methods.text: Mapped the current and proposed journeys for the website and app, then restructured the IA to separate explanation from conversion.

methods.title: Personas
methods.text: A protagonist and a cast of seven, across the three segments, used to test every decision against different ages, needs and attitudes to therapy.

interviews.lead: Eight one-on-one interviews of about 30 minutes, held in Italian and recorded with consent, one or more in each segment. They covered how people look for a therapist, what makes a platform feel trustworthy and what stops them from starting.

quotes.text: Starting therapy with someone who turns out not to be right is just more lost time for a person who is already fragile.
Too much choice, too much choice. How do you tell if someone is right for you? I was having so many panic attacks, I don’t think I could have done it.
Being able to read the doctor’s CV, their history. I want it to be clear.
Reviews helped up to a point. The first person I found wasn’t the right one, even with good reviews.
More than anything it should feel serious. I need to know I’m talking to serious people.

themes.title: Help comes late, and in a hurry
themes.text: Almost everyone waits until things feel overwhelming, so the first visit happens under urgency and fatigue.
themes.design: A crisis banner on every questionnaire screen and a short guided path

themes.title: Too much choice
themes.text: Long therapist lists are impossible to judge without experience, and harder still when distressed.
themes.design: Three curated proposals with “why we suggest them”; browsing stays available

themes.title: Fit over credentials
themes.text: Feeling listened to matters more than age, gender or method, but people want to know the approach before they start.
themes.design: Approach, experience and first slot on every card, plus a free introductory call

themes.title: Transparency builds trust
themes.text: CVs, clear prices, reviews and an honest explanation of how matching works.
themes.design: Pricing on the home screen and a “why this match” note on each proposal

themes.title: Nothing should feel final
themes.text: Changing therapist or redoing the questionnaire without penalty lowers the fear of committing.
themes.design: Change therapist without retaking the whole test

themes.title: Calm, not clinical
themes.text: Soft colours and rounded shapes; neither hospital-like nor a playful wellness app.
themes.design: A restrained palette, one accent and gentle motion

cast.lead: One protagonist and seven supporting personas, built from the interviews and spread across the three age segments and stages of change. Each is rated 1-5 on six traits, so the cast shows where the design has to stretch.

members.name: Luca Taglioni
members.quote: There is hope, even when your brain tells you there isn't.
members.summary: Anxiety, panic attacks and poor sleep, mostly from work pressure. Friends in therapy encouraged him and he feels ready. He expects polished, personal apps and dislikes rigid, bureaucratic flows. He will invest time and money if the platform feels trustworthy and human.
members.useCase: On a Sunday morning Luca opens the app a friend recommended, filters for therapists who work on anxiety and stress, compares availability, takes the questionnaire and books a free introductory session for later that week.
needs: A clean, professional interface that still feels warm, not clinical
Filters and recommendations tailored to anxiety and sleep
Booking with availability, cost and policies up front
Reassuring microcopy for a first-time therapy user

members.name: Giulia Romitelli
members.quote: I am proud of the woman I am today, because I went through one hell of a time becoming her.
members.summary: Two children, a full-time job and years of chronic stress. Therapy feels like one more thing to manage, and she feels guilty spending on herself.

members.name: Alessandro Rigoni
members.quote: The hardest part isn’t talking, it’s believing that it’s safe to begin.
members.summary: Digitally skilled but emotionally cautious. He opens the app, reads testimonials and closes it again. One bad first interaction could push him away for years.
needs: Signals that he can stop at any time
Clear explanations of what happens next

members.name: Sara Locci
members.quote: I’ve done the work before. What I’m looking for now is the right place to continue it.
members.summary: Two past therapies, one good and one disappointing. She knows what she needs and leaves anything that feels generic or repetitive.
needs: Matching on approach and past experience

members.name: Chiara Ronchi
members.quote: I’ve learned to live in another language, but I still need to feel understood in my own.
members.summary: Living abroad for six years, fluent in English and German but emotionally tied to Italian. Local therapy feels culturally distant.

members.name: Marco Sorcinelli
members.quote: Trust is not built by promises, but by knowing who stands behind them.
members.summary: Stress, irritability and loneliness he would not call psychological problems. He trusts credentials and institutions, not apps.
needs: Visible credentials and a professional tone

members.name: Antonio Longo
members.quote: I don’t need something advanced. I need something I can rely on.
members.summary: Ten years of chronic back pain and low mood. Limited mobility makes commuting hard, and complex interfaces frustrate him.
needs: Reassurance that he did it right

members.name: Paola Giacomini
members.quote: I don’t need the perfect solution. I need someone before I fall apart.
members.summary: Recently divorced and in an unprecedented depressive episode. She cannot wait weeks or compare dozens of profiles; she needs someone now.
needs: A priority path with fast matching

requirements.title: Build trust immediately, on several levels

flows.caption: 01 · Onboarding and discovery: from first contact to an informed choice of path
02 · Matching questionnaire: one question at a time, visible progress, support always at hand
03 · Professionals portal: browse, filter and compare profiles independently
04 · Proposals and booking: three explained proposals, booking in two taps, clear payment
05 · Personal area: next appointment first, chat, diary and agenda in a floating tab bar
06 · Online session: from device check to feedback without leaving the app
07 · Between sessions: short guided practices and a private view of progress, suggested by the therapist

motion.caption: Splash: portraits pop in one by one, then the message and actions rise
Guided breathing: the circle expands, holds and releases while the cue changes
Section completed: the next petal blooms in, and after the third section the Unobravo mark is whole
Living illustrations: the figures sway, heads bob and the breath rises on a slow three-second loop
Booking confirmed: the check springs in with a soft pulse, then the details rise one after another
Video session: controls slide in and the live indicator pulses

prototype.text: The full prototype is wired in Figma as one continuous prototype, from first visit to the video session: about 250 connections across seven flows, with interactive answer options, filter sheets and smart-animated questionnaire progress. Try it below, or open it in Figma.

system.text: Behind the screens is a small design system: 46 variables, 14 text styles, 34 components, 47 icons and ten illustrations. Fifteen primitives feed seventeen semantic tokens, and every fill has exactly one job: coral is the only action colour, a coral tint marks selection, clay holds information, sage means something went well, and crimson is kept for errors. Icons are drawn in warm clay and ink, like the text around them, and only turn coral when active. Screens sit on flat paper, with no gradient.

illustrations.meta: Petali: ten scenes built from the Unobravo mark
illustrations.lead: The logo is two people: two round heads over two leaning bodies, a shade darker where they overlap. Every illustration is made from those parts only: soft rounded bodies in apricot and sand, heads, and the gentle overprint where they meet. Coral is kept for small accents. No suns, plants or mugs: each scene is a small arrangement of people, and the questionnaire ends with the mark itself assembling.

results.text: Four participants completed every task on the final version, working alone while recording their screen, with no errors. Scores also became more consistent as the design matured (variance fell from 58.33 to 29.69). Participants singled out the “why this therapist” explanation as what made the matching feel trustworthy.

reflection: The biggest change was structural, not visual: separating “understand the service” from “start the test” fixed three critical issues at once. For a mental-health service, trust comes from transparency: showing how matching works, what it costs and what happens to your data.

The final version adds what a real product would need next: crisis support and health-data consent in the questionnaire, empty and error states, and the online session itself. The samples were small (three to four people per round), so the next step would be a larger test across all age segments.

beforeAfterPairs.lead: Screenshots of the original app next to the redesign, screen by screen. Each pair notes what changed and which usability issue it answers.

pairs.label: Welcome
pairs.before: The first screen: a decorative landscape, a language picker and two buttons, with no idea yet of what the service is.
pairs.after: One welcome with real therapists and two clear paths: learn how it works, or start.

pairs.label: Questionnaire
pairs.before: A long checklist under a decorative landscape, a faint back link and a disabled next button.
pairs.after: Section progress, one question at a time, and emergency support one tap away on every screen.

pairs.label: Proposals
pairs.before: One therapist per swipe: a large photo, a name and little else to compare.
pairs.after: Three proposals side by side with approach, languages, first slot and price, plus why each was suggested.

pairs.label: Booking
pairs.before: A week strip with no sign of availability; unavailable preferences give no feedback.
pairs.after: A month view with the chosen day and time, repeated in the button that confirms it.

pairs.label: Home
pairs.before: Navigation hidden in a sidebar and a list of generic next steps.
pairs.after: The next appointment comes first, a short practice is suggested, and a floating tab bar reaches everything.

pairs.label: Change therapist
pairs.before: A dialog that sends you back to the whole questionnaire whatever the reason.
pairs.after: Choose what to change: only preferences, a short retake, or browse profiles yourself.

pairs.label: Chat
pairs.before: An automated summary of your answers dominates the conversation.
pairs.after: A plain conversation with the therapist, with the usual response time shown in the header.

project.context: HCI course project, MA Digital Humanities and Digital Knowledge, University of Bologna

summary.brief: People hesitate to start online therapy: how the service works, matching, prices and privacy were hard to understand.
summary.role: Solo: research, UX and UI design, prototyping and testing.
summary.method: Interviews, expert review and think-aloud tests; three design iterations; a summative usability test.
summary.outcome: SUS rose from 75 to 91.25, with 100% task success and zero errors (4 participants).

facts: participants finished every task, no errors
project.shows: Trust through transparency: research, three iterations and a measured gain in usability.

decisions.choice: Separate explaining the service from starting the test, instead of tidying the existing “How it works” page.
decisions.why: No tested user could explain how Unobravo works, and the calls to action dropped people into the questionnaire when they expected an explanation.
decisions.result: One structural change fixed three critical issues at once; in the final test every participant understood the service in about a minute and a half.

decisions.choice: Always offer three therapists, each with a “why we chose this therapist for you” explanation.
decisions.why: Matching was opaque: the promised three profiles never arrived, and users had to retake the test.
decisions.result: Participants singled out the explanation as what made the matching feel trustworthy.

decisions.choice: Let people change their schedule or preferences without retaking the questionnaire.
decisions.why: Users repeated the whole test just to change their availability.
decisions.result: Changing therapist for scheduling took about 25 seconds, with no errors.

decisions.choice: Replace the app’s sidebar with a tab bar and a dashboard.
decisions.why: Navigation was hidden in the sidebar, and there was nowhere to see the next appointment or the therapy so far.
decisions.result: Comparing and changing therapist, a task every user failed on the original app, took about 30 seconds.
